name: そば処 更科
cuisine: A 1930s neighbourhood soba shop where half the room orders the ramen: hand-cut soba and donburi at ¥800–¥1,150, and an ¥800 chūka-soba whose broth is pork bone, chicken frame and negi only — no fish, no tare-shop tricks — over noodles made in-house. Cash only, everything under ¥1,200.
neighborhood: Shinjuku 1-chōme, on the quiet residential stretch between Shinjuku Gyoen and Yasukuni-dōri — 230 m / 3–5 min from Shinjuku-gyoemmae (Tokyo Metro Marunouchi line, exit 1 or 3); about 1 km east of Shinjuku Station, so the light record's 「新宿駅周辺」 was off
gf_detail: Wheat is everywhere and there is no gluten-free anything. The soba is not jūwari and no source claims it is, so assume the usual nihachi wheat binder plus wheat dusting flour on the board; the ramen and the chūka-soba are wheat egg noodles made in the same kitchen; the tsuyu, the katsudon and oyakodon broths and the curry roux are all built on ordinary wheat soy sauce; katsu and tempura come out of a shared fryer with a flour-and-panko coat. Nobody here has ever advertised allergen handling, the shop takes no reservations, and orders are shouted across a two-floor room at lunch — this is not a place to attempt a celiac negotiation.
vegan_detail: Not viable. The soba tsuyu is a bonito-and-soy dashi, the ramen broth is explicitly pork bone and chicken frame, and the rice bowls are egg-bound pork or chicken. Even a plain zaru arrives with a fish dipping sauce. No plant-based option is published and none is likely to be improvised.

roles: owner-operated neighbourhood soba shop, run by the same family since the 1930s
chef_bio.origin: Shinjuku 1-chōme, Shinjuku-ku — the shop has stood on this block since before the war
chef_bio.background: The interesting thing about this shop is that it is a soba shop famous for ramen. Tabelog records its opening year as 1935; a detailed Japanese write-up puts it at 1936 and says the ramen has been made the same way for more than seventy years — the recipe was handed over just after the war by the owner of a neighbouring Chinese restaurant, and the shop never changed it. What makes it worth the walk is the refusal to modernise: where most soba shops that added ramen now build a fish-and-dashi hybrid broth out of the soba kitchen, 更科 takes its stock from 豚骨・鶏ガラ・ネギのみ — pork bone, chicken carcass and spring onion, nothing else — and cuts the noodles in-house, so they carry the fresh, faintly soba-ish snap of a shop that makes its own. It was put on the cover of one of Hidekazu Ishigami's ramen books, which is why regulars queue for an ¥800 bowl in a room that still looks like a 1970s shokudō, and why roughly half the customers walk past sixty-odd soba items to order it. The menu is deliberately vast for a shop this size — zaru and tanuki soba at ¥800, okame soba with a whole shiitake at ¥900, curry nanban ¥950, ramen ¥800, chāshū-men ¥1,100, oyakodon ¥1,050, katsudon ¥1,100, katsu curry ¥1,150, with a ¥350 mini curry and ¥400 kayaku-gohan to bolt on. Two floors, table seating only, a TV on the ground floor, wooden chopsticks, shichimi and pepper on the table, cash settled after you eat. Weekday lunch and early dinner only; the shop shuts entirely at weekends and on public holidays, which is the giveaway that it lives off the office blocks around Shinjuku Gyoen rather than off tourists.
chef_bio.philosophy: Change nothing. A post-war ramen recipe borrowed from the Chinese restaurant next door, kept unaltered for seventy years, sold at the same price as the zaru.
chef_bio.specialty: ラーメン ¥800 — pork-bone/chicken/negi broth with house-made noodles, no fish; チャーシューメン ¥1,100; おかめそば ¥900; Cセット (ramen + mini curry rice); かやくごはん ¥400.

anecdotes.text: The ramen is not the shop's own invention: the recipe came from the owner of a Chinese restaurant nearby in the years right after the war, and has been made unchanged for over seventy years.
Where other soba shops fold fish dashi into their ramen, this one takes the stock from pork bone, chicken carcass and negi only — 「豚骨・鶏ガラ・ネギのみでダシを取った」.

A Tabelog regular's summary of the trap: 「創業一世紀に迫る老舗で蕎麦前 → 蕎麦無し」 — you come to an almost-century-old soba house and leave without eating soba. Another notes the shop's ramen made the cover of an Ishigami ramen guide.
Do not confuse it with the other 更科 in the same district: 更科 at 新宿2-16-11 サンフタミビル 1F, three minutes from Shinjuku-sanchōme, is a separate shop with different hours.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog supplies the address (新宿1-30-5 1F), phone 03-3351-2951, coordinates, the 1935 opening year, weekday-only hours, 予約不可, cash-only payment, all-non-smoking and a 50-seat count. Retty gives the same address, phone and hours but counts 32 seats over two floors (20 upstairs of the split, 12 on the other) — the two sources disagree and neither was verified on site. The masaemon write-up supplies the 1936 founding claim, the post-war Chinese-restaurant provenance of the ramen, the seventy-years-unchanged claim, the pork-bone/chicken/negi stock and the house-made noodles. A menu-survey site lists the current prices and confirms cash-only, table-only seating.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One kitchen boils soba, udon and wheat ramen noodles and runs a fryer for katsu and tempura. Nothing is separated and nothing is claimed to be.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard soba-shop tsuyu, donburi broths and curry — all ordinary wheat soy sauce. No tamari or wheat-free soy is mentioned anywhere.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bonito dashi in the soba tsuyu; the ramen stock is pork bone and chicken frame; katsu and oyakodon are egg-bound pork and chicken.

positives.text: All seats non-smoking, two floors so the lunch queue moves, and nothing on the menu tops ¥1,150.

cultural_comfort.note: A weekday office-district shokudō with no English published, no reservations, no cards, no e-money and no QR payment — bring cash and pay after you eat. Ordering is verbal at a table; the menu runs to sixty -odd items on Japanese-only strips. It is quiet, entirely non-smoking, easy to enter alone and used to solo diners, and the ramen is easy to point at. Closed all weekend and on public holidays, so a visitor planning around it needs a weekday between 11:30–15:00 or 17:30–20:30.

enrich_note: CONFIRMED. Exact name match to Tabelog 13094274, 新宿区新宿1-30-5 1F, phone 03-3351-2951, corroborated by Retty and by two independent Japanese write-ups. Coordinates moved from the neighbourhood centroid to the shop (35.689984/139.712631) and loc_precise set true; the light record's 「新宿駅周辺」 was wrong — it is a Shinjuku-gyoemmae shop about 1 km east of Shinjuku Station. The light record's GF 'ask' / vegan 'limited' are both downgraded to 'no': the soba is not jūwari, the ramen and chūka-soba are wheat, and every sauce in the house is wheat soy. CAUTION for the merge: there is a second, unrelated 更科 at 新宿2-16-11 near Shinjuku-sanchōme — do not merge them.

name: トンテキ食堂 なかむら
address_ja: 東京都新宿区新宿3-3-9 伍名館 B1F
cuisine: A basement pork-steak counter a minute off Shinjuku-sanchōme: thick tonteki in a dark sweet-savoury sauce, with obanzai side dishes made from vegetables the owners grow themselves. Roughly ¥1,000–¥2,000 at lunch, ¥2,000–¥3,000 if you drink.
neighborhood: Shinjuku 3-chōme, basement of the Gomeikan building — 120 m / 1 min from Shinjuku-sanchōme station exit C4 (Tokyo Metro Marunouchi & Fukutoshin lines, Toei Shinjuku line)
gf_detail: No gluten-free claim of any kind, and the dish itself is the problem: tonteki is defined by its sauce, which in every published version of the dish is built on soy sauce and Worcestershire — both wheat — usually with oyster sauce or mirin behind it. Nothing on the shop's own Instagram or its Tabelog page mentions allergens, tamari or wheat-free seasoning. The obanzai sides are seasoned from the same soy-based pantry. Treat this as a no.
vegan_detail: The shop describes itself in one line — 「食材にこだわりました。豚ステーキのお店です」, a pork steak shop — so the centre of the menu is out. The vegetable obanzai the owners make from their own field are genuinely the good part of the room and Tabelog flags 野菜料理にこだわる, but Japanese obanzai are routinely seasoned with bonito dashi and soy, and no plant-based claim is published. Do not assume.

chef_bio.background: A twenty-five-seat basement room that opened in March 2020, which is to say it opened into the first state of emergency and survived it. The concept is narrow on purpose: tonteki — the thick pan-seared pork steak that Yokkaichi in Mie made famous — plus drink, plus vegetables. The shop's own line is 「トンテキとお酒と、ときどき野菜。育てた野菜で作る。」: they grow produce themselves and build the obanzai sides from what comes off the field, which is an unusual amount of effort for a ¥1,000-lunch basement in Shinjuku. Practicalities: 25 seats with a counter, all non-smoking, standing drinking allowed, free Wi-Fi, no reservations, cards not accepted but PayPay is, children welcome, delivery via RocketNow, closing days irregular. It is not, whatever the light record implied, an old Shōwa-era shokudō.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「トンテキとお酒と、ときどき野菜。育てた野菜で作る。」 — pork steak, a drink, and vegetables they grew.
chef_bio.specialty: Tonteki (thick pork steak); obanzai side dishes from the owners' own vegetables; sake and wine list.

anecdotes.text: Instagram bio, in full: 「食材にこだわりました。豚ステーキのお店です」 — a pork steak shop that is fussy about ingredients.
Tabelog records the opening date as 16 March 2020, 25 seats, all non-smoking, no reservations, cards not accepted but PayPay yes.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog gives the address (新宿3-3-9 伍名館 B1F), coordinates, phone 03-5315-4511, hours, opening date, seat count, payment methods and the shop's own PR text about growing its vegetables. The shop's Instagram confirms the address and the one-line self-description. No third-party interview or press coverage was found, so there is no named chef and no verified biography.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tonteki sauce is soy-and-Worcestershire based by definition and the shop names no alternative seasoning; the obanzai come from the same pantry.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A pork-steak specialist: the pan, the sauce and the room are all built around pork.

positives.text: All-non-smoking, counter seating, free Wi-Fi, children welcome, PayPay accepted, open to 22:00 (23:00 Fri/Sat) — an easy solo room.

cultural_comfort.note: One minute from Shinjuku-sanchōme exit C4, down into a basement. Small (25 seats) and counter-heavy, so solo diners fit; all non-smoking; free Wi-Fi; children allowed. No reservations taken. Credit cards are NOT accepted — cash or PayPay only. No English menu is advertised, but 'tonteki' is one word and the menu is short. Closing days are irregular, so check the Instagram before making the trip.

enrich_note: NAME CORRECTION (inferential — flagging for the human pass). The light record read 「トンテキ 新宿」, which is a description, not a business name; no restaurant is registered under it. chef_bio.background: Could not be established, because the branch does not exist and the name conflates two different companies. 小諸そば is real: a 株式会社三ッ和 brand approaching its fiftieth year, roughly 60,000 customers a day, self-milled/self-made noodles, kake at ¥390. Its Shinjuku-area branches are 小諸そば 新宿南口店, 小諸そば 新宿一丁目店 and 小諸そば 代々木店 — Tabelog's nationwide 小諸そば search and its Shinjuku-area search both return that set and nothing called メトロピア. 「メトロピア」, meanwhile, is not a Shinjuku place at all: it is Tokyo Metro Properties' brand for its underground station malls, and the soba tenant in those malls is a different chain, そば処 めとろ庵, whose メトロピア branches are 大手町, 錦糸町, 新木場 and 西船橋. There is no めとろ庵 in Shinjuku and no メトロピア at Shinjuku Station. The name in the light record is a composite that has never existed.

name: 新宿西口思い出横丁
cuisine: Not a restaurant but a lane: about eighty tiny businesses, some sixty of them food and drink, packed into roughly 630 tsubo beside Shinjuku Station's west exit. Mostly motsu-yaki and yakitori counters of six to ten seats, charcoal smoke, standing room, beer and shōchū, a few hundred yen a skewer.
neighborhood: Nishi-Shinjuku 1-2, immediately north-west of the Shinjuku Station west exit — under a minute from the JR west exit, ~70 m from Seibu-Shinjuku station, and adjacent to the Ōdakyū/Keiō and Marunouchi line concourses
hours_raw: 店舗により異なる（営業日・営業時間・メニューは各店舗ごとに異なり、予告なく変更される場合があります）
gf_detail: Structurally unsafe and there is nothing to negotiate with. The lane's staple trades are motsu-yaki and yakitori, which means tare — a wheat-soy-sauce glaze — brushed and re-dipped over a shared charcoal grill, plus ramen, gyōza, oden and udon counters within arm's reach. Individual shops are six to ten seats with one cook, no allergen documentation, and mostly Japanese-only; the site itself warns that menus differ by shop and change without notice. No shop in the lane advertises gluten-free handling. A celiac should treat the whole alley as off-limits rather than try to find an exception inside it.
vegan_detail: The lane exists to grill offal and chicken. Even the vegetable skewers go on the same grill and into the same tare, the ramen and udon counters run bonito or pork stock, and there is no plant-based venue among the ~60 food businesses on the official directory.

roles: a shōtengai / alley association, not a single business
chef_bio.origin: Nishi-Shinjuku 1-2, Shinjuku-ku — grew out of the post-war open-air stall market on the burnt-out ground beside Shinjuku Station
chef_bio.background: Omoide-yokochō — 'Memory Lane' — is the surviving fragment of the black-market stall district that formed on the bombed ground at Shinjuku's west exit right after the war. The official association describes it as 「戦後直後に焼け野原にできた露天商のマーケット」 that hardened into a permanent lane: today roughly eighty businesses on about 630 tsubo (~2,080 m²), of which around sixty are food and drink, and the trade is overwhelmingly motsu-yaki and yakitori. What a visitor actually gets is a pair of alleys barely wide enough for two people, low doorways, counters of six to ten stools, charcoal smoke that gets into your coat, and shops that open and close at their own hours — the association explicitly says 営業日や営業時間、メニューなど vary by shop and change without notice. It is a genuine piece of Shōwa Tokyo rather than a reconstruction, and it is also one of the most photographed lanes in the city, so evenings are crowded and some shops post cover charges. The association runs its own site with English, Chinese and Korean versions.
chef_bio.specialty: Motsu-yaki and yakitori counters; also ramen, soba, gyōza, oden and standing bars.

anecdotes.text: The association's own framing: 「ノスタルジックな情景が残る、古き良き飲屋街」 — a nostalgic, old-fashioned drinking street, descended from the post-war street-vendor market.
Scale, from the official site: roughly 630 tsubo of land, about 80 businesses, about 60 of them food and drink, centred on motsu-yaki and yakitori.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The 新宿西口思い出横丁 association's official site supplies the history, the land area, the shop counts, the trade mix and the warning that hours and menus vary by shop; it also carries English, Chinese and Korean pages. Tabelog listings for individual tenants (もつ焼き ウッチャン 新宿思い出横丁 at 西新宿1-2-7, かっぺ亭 新宿思い出横丁本店 at 西新宿1-2-1) fix the block and the coordinates.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Six-to-ten-seat counters, one grill, tare re-used across skewers; ramen, udon and gyōza counters in the same lane. No shop publishes allergen handling.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Yakitori and motsu-yaki tare is wheat soy sauce by default, and no shop in the lane names a gluten-free tamari.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Offal and chicken on a shared charcoal grill; vegetable skewers cook over the same fat.

positives.text: The association publishes English, Chinese and Korean versions of its shop directory and map.

cultural_comfort.note: Physically easy to reach — a minute from the JR west exit — and hard to be comfortable in. Counters seat six to ten, shops are Japanese-speaking, smoking is common, some charge a cover, cash dominates, and at night the lane is shoulder-to-shoulder with photographers. Lunch and early evening are much easier than 21:00. The association's multilingual site and map are the practical way in, but every individual shop sets its own days, hours and menu and can change them without notice. Go for the atmosphere; do not go with a dietary requirement.

enrich_note: CATEGORY FLAG — needs a human decision. 新宿西口思い出横丁 is real and correctly located, but it is a lane of ~80 businesses, not a single restaurant, and it is filed here as MOM_AND_POP with a name (「新宿思い出横丁」) that is the district rather than a shop. Either recategorise it as a district/area entry or delete it and replace it with specific tenants. Coordinates corrected from the neighbourhood centroid to the lane itself (35.6932/139.6996, 西新宿1-2), triangulated from two Tabelog tenant listings inside it; loc_precise set true because the address is real, though it denotes a block rather than a door. GF moved from 'ask' to 'no' — a motsu-yaki/yakitori alley of single-cook counters with shared tare is not a place to ask.

gf_detail: Not assessed, because the shop is not identified. Standing note that applies to all three candidates: the Sarashina houses are famous for 更科そば, the pale noodle cut from the inner core of the buckwheat seed — which is precisely the style that needs the most wheat binder. None of them is jūwari, all of them serve tempura, and all of them dip in wheat-soy tsuyu. A 更科 shop is one of the least gluten-free soba styles there is, and no reader should take the name as reassurance.
vegan_detail: Not assessed. Sarashina tsuyu is a bonito-and-soy dashi at all three candidate shops.

chef_bio.background: Deliberately not written, because the record cannot be pinned to one business. Two things are certain. First, the pin is wrong: 「麻布十番 更科」 names Azabu-Jūban in Minato-ku, while this record sits at Takadanobaba in Shinjuku-ku, about 6 km north-west, and a Tabelog keyword search of the whole Takadanobaba/Ikebukuro area (A1305) for 更科 returns no 更科 soba shop there at all (only a 永坂更科 布屋太兵衛 department-store counter in Ikebukuro). Second, no business is registered under the exact string 「麻布十番 更科」; instead Azabu-Jūban holds three separate and historically rival Sarashina houses, any of which a sweep could have flattened into that name: (a) 総本家更科堀井 本店, 港区元麻布3-11-4, 35.656811/139.732890, 286 m from Azabu-Jūban station, 70 seats, 11:30–15:00 / 17:00–20:00 weekdays and 11:00–20:00 weekends, dinner budget ¥5,000–5,999; (b) 麻布永坂 更科本店, 港区麻布十番1-2-7, 35.656585/139.736774, 68 m from the station, 88 seats, 11:00–21:30, closed Wednesdays, dinner budget ¥3,000–3,999; (c) 永坂更科 布屋太兵衛 麻布総本店, 港区麻布十番1-8-7, 35.655785/139.735790, 85 m from the station, 11:00–20:00 daily. Two of the three are literally addressed in Azabu-Jūban 1-chōme, so 'the one in Azabu-Jūban' does not disambiguate. No substitution has been made.
